entry.title: Four Numbers, Monday Aug 31: 27, 134-155, 60 and 41
entry.summary: A new Monday column. One number for each Detroit club. The Tigers have blown more saves than they have converted and only 2 other teams in baseball can say that. The Lions open in 13 days against a schedule whose opponents went 134-155 last year. The Pistons won 60. The Red Wings won 41 again.
entry.content:
This runs Monday mornings. One number for each of the Tigers, Lions, Pistons and Red Wings, whichever one is worth knowing that week, with the arithmetic shown so you can check it.

Tigers: 27

27 saves. 28 blown. 55 chances, and they've converted fewer than half of them.

Three clubs in baseball have blown more saves than they've converted this season, and Detroit is one of them. Here are the 5 worst conversion rates in the league; the top 3 rows are those 3 clubs.

The part that makes it strange is the company Detroit isn't keeping. The Angels have a bad pitching staff. Washington has a bad pitching staff. Detroit has the 5th best team ERA in baseball at 3.58, behind the Yankees, Milwaukee, Atlanta and Boston and ahead of 25 other clubs.

That's the whole season in 2 rows. 596 runs scored, 531 allowed, a plus 65 that should be worth something, and a 63-73 record that isn't. Sunday was a version of it in miniature: Framber Valdez left down 3-1 and Tanner Rainey turned it into 6-1 in a third of an inning.

Good pitching. Handed back after the 7th.

Lions: 134-155

That's the 2025 record of the 17 teams on Detroit's 2026 schedule, added up. A .464 winning percentage. Only 3 teams in the league drew a softer one: Cleveland at .429, New Orleans at .433 and Cincinnati at .450. Detroit is level with Atlanta and Indianapolis at .464, so call it 4th easiest of 32 in a 3 way tie.

5 of the 17 are against clubs that won 6 games or fewer last year. Three of them went 3-14. On the other side there are only 4 games against teams that won 11 or more, and 2 of those are the Chicago games.

Now the honest part, because last year's record is a weak instrument. It's the same lesson the preseason numbers teach: teams turn over, and what a club did in January tells you less about September than the confidence with which people quote it. Six of these games are against Green Bay, Minnesota and Chicago, and nobody needs a 2025 record to know those are hard.

What the number does say is that the soft part of this schedule is real and it is front loaded. The Jets, Carolina and Arizona in weeks 3, 4 and 5, with the bye in week 6. If Detroit is not comfortably over .500 by Halloween, the schedule will not have been the reason.

Pistons: 60

60-22. The most games the Pistons have won in a season since 2005-06, when they won 64.

Two years before that, they won 14.

Red Wings: 41

41 wins in 82 games. They also won 41 in 2024, and 41 in 2016.

Since 2015 the Red Wings have never won more than 41 games in a season. Three times they've landed on exactly 41, which is the kind of consistency nobody wants.

The hockey caveat matters here: an overtime loss is a loss in that win column but it's a point in the standings, so 41-41 understates a Red Wings season a little. It understates all 3 of them by about the same amount, which is why they still line up.

Both seasons start in October. This is the last quiet Monday either of them gets.

entry.title: Graded: Pick No. 18. The unnamed starter turned out to be Tyler Glasnow
entry.summary: The call was Dodgers win, High, and the one thing named as a risk was that Los Angeles had not announced a Sunday starter. They handed it to Tyler Glasnow, who went 7 innings on 85 pitches. Detroit got 2 hits, which ties its season low. Final: Dodgers 6, Tigers 1.
entry.content:
The call, committed before first pitch: Dodgers win. Confidence High.

The result: Dodgers 6, Tigers 1. gamePk 824232, Final on the id.

Record: 10-8.

The risk the entry named was the only thing it got wrong about

Saturday morning, when this went on the board, the entry said the whole risk was that Los Angeles hadn't announced anybody for Sunday, and that a bullpen game the day after Blake Snell is exactly the sort of afternoon Detroit steals.

They didn't use a bullpen game. They used Tyler Glasnow.

Tyler Glasnow, Sunday7.0 IP2 H1 R1 BB6 K85 pitches

85 pitches through 7 is a starter who was never in trouble. Kyle Hurt and Seth Halvorsen finished it off without allowing a hit between them.

Detroit got 2 hits, and that is a number worth sitting with

Gleyber Torres had one. Kevin McGonigle had the other, and drove in the only run in the 4th. That was the offense.

2 hits ties Detroit's season low, and it is the 6th time they've done it in 2026. Two of those 6 have come in the last 5 days: the 3-0 loss to Tampa Bay on Aug 26 and this one.

Only 4 men left on base, which sounds like efficiency and isn't. You cannot strand runners you never put on.

Valdez was fine. It didn't matter

The entry's worry about Framber Valdez was his 1.41 WHIP, 56 walks in 144.2 innings, a pitcher who hands out traffic against a lineup that had scored 663 runs.

He walked 1. He went 6, gave up 3, threw 105 pitches, and took the loss because his team managed 2 hits.

Framber Valdez, Sunday6.0 IP6 H3 ER1 BB5 K105 pitches

The game was 3-1 when he left. It ended 6-1 because Tanner Rainey came in for the 8th, got 1 out, and gave up 2 hits and 2 walks for 3 runs. Kyle Finnegan had to put the fire out and Jacob Waguespack threw a clean 9th.

Where this leaves them

Detroit is 63-73 with 596 runs scored and 531 allowed. Los Angeles left town 82-55 after taking 2 of 3.

The Tigers won the middle game of that series 2-1 and lost the other two by a combined 8-2. That is the season in one weekend: they hang around, they don't score, and one inning gets away.

Minnesota is next, starting tonight at Target Field, and that pick is already on the board.

Not betting advice.

entry.title: Series preview: Minnesota has allowed 156 more runs than Detroit and is still ahead of them in the standings
entry.summary: Detroit is 63-72 having allowed 525 runs. Minnesota is 64-72 having allowed 681. The whole difference is what happens in a one-run game: Detroit is 13-23 in them and has converted 27 of 55 save chances, 2nd worst in baseball. Monday: Tigers win, Low. The series: Detroit takes 2 of 3.
entry.content:
Detroit at Minnesota. Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday, all 7:40pm ET at Target Field. Monday: Tigers win. The series: Detroit takes 2 of 3.

Here are 2 clubs separated by half a game.

RecordRuns scoredRuns allowedDiff
Minnesota64-72621681-60
Detroit63-72595525+70

156 runs of separation in run prevention, and Minnesota is the one in front. Half a game, with Detroit holding a game in hand, so it's very nearly nothing, and both of these teams have played themselves out of the race anyway. But a 130 run swing in differential should buy more than nothing.

It buys nothing here, and the reason is the thing that has defined Detroit's whole season.

The division is normal. Detroit isn't.

The same numbers, for anyone who would rather read them:

AL CentralRecordRSRAExpected winsAbove or below
Twins64-7262168162.3+1.7

Royals62-7558966261.2+0.8
White Sox72-6365160372.2-0.2
Tigers63-7259552575.2-12.2

Pythagorean exponent 1.83, which is Baseball Reference's standard. Four teams in this division sit within 2 wins of what their runs say they should have. The fifth is 12 under, and it's the only one in the group with a positive run differential.

That -12.2 is the largest gap in baseball. Second place is the Angels at -7.7, and they at least have the decency to be bad at everything.

Where the 12 wins went

TigersTwins
Team ERA3.564.68
WHIP1.221.39
Saves2738
Blown saves2816
Record in 1-run games13-2314-20
Record in extra innings4-74-3

Detroit has blown more saves than it has converted. 27 for 55 is the 2nd worst conversion rate in the major leagues, behind only the Angels, and it's being posted by the staff with the best ERA in this division. Minnesota's pitchers give up more than a full run a game more than Detroit's and convert 38 of 54.

13-23 in one-run games is the same fact told as wins and losses. Detroit has played 36 of them, more than a quarter of its season, and lost 23. You don't need a model to turn 156 runs of pitching advantage into nothing. You just need to keep handing 1-run leads back in the 8th.

The season series says the opposite, and it's 7 games

Minnesota has won 5 of 7. Detroit has outscored them anyway.

DateScoreWhere
Apr 6Detroit 3, Minnesota 7at Minnesota
Apr 7Detroit 2, Minnesota 4at Minnesota
Apr 8Detroit 6, Minnesota 8at Minnesota
Apr 9Detroit 1, Minnesota 3at Minnesota
Jun 9Detroit 10, Minnesota 4at Detroit
Jun 10Detroit 4, Minnesota 6at Detroit
Jun 11Detroit 11, Minnesota 0at Detroit

37 runs to 32, and 21 of Detroit's 37 came in the 2 games it won. That isn't a mystery, it's the 1-run game problem wearing an April jersey: 4 games at Target Field, 4 losses, 3 of them by exactly 2 runs.

What Minnesota is missing

Joe Ryan is on the 15-day injured list. 125.2 innings, 3.65 ERA, and on a staff whose team number is 4.68 he's the one starter who has been meaningfully better than the group. Austin Martin is on the 10-day.

None of the 3 starters for this series had been named as of Sunday morning, on either side, so this is a team-level call rather than a matchup one and I'd rather say that than pretend I know who's throwing.

Detroit's own list is worse and has been for 2 weeks. Riley Greene, Kerry Carpenter and Matt Vierling are all out, which is an outfield, and Greene was an .816 OPS over 492 plate appearances. Jack Flaherty is on the 15-day.

The call

Tigers win Monday. Low.

The case is that Minnesota has to score to win and this Detroit pitching staff is the reason nobody in this division scores on it. 525 runs allowed in 135 games is 3.9 a night. Minnesota gives up 5.0. Over 3 games, the club allowing a run less per game should take the series, and that's why the series call is Detroit in 2 of 3 even with the head to head pointing the other way.

The series: Detroit takes 2 of 3.

And here's the number that argues hardest against all of that, because it's the only sample of this exact matchup in this exact park: in those 4 April games at Target Field, Detroit allowed 22 runs. 5.5 a game, from the staff this whole piece has been calling the best in the division, and worse than the 5.0 Minnesota gives up on the season.

4 games is 4 games and I'm not going to build a pick on it. But I'm also not going to quote a season average at you and quietly skip the one slice of it that was played where Monday's game is going to be played.

What scares me

Everything about how Detroit has actually been playing.

2-8 in its last 10. 29-38 on the road. 3-9 over the last 14 days. A .239 team average with 3 outfielders on the injured list, and the last 2 weeks have been full of nights where Detroit got 6 hits and lost. Saturday it got 6 hits and won, and that felt like an exception rather than a turn.

And the mechanism hasn't been fixed. Nothing about this morning says the bullpen that's 27 for 55 has stopped being 27 for 55. If Monday is 2-1 in the 7th, all of the above is a good argument that loses anyway, which is what a 12 win gap is: a good argument losing 36 times.

It's Low because I think Detroit is the better team and I've watched the better team lose this exact game since April.

Not betting advice.

6 hits. 12 men left on base. A ground-rule double from Gleyber Torres in the 3rd, then nothing for 5 innings, then Freddie Freeman singled Alek Thomas home in the 6th to tie it, then nothing again until the 9th.

That is a club that scored 2 runs on 6 hits and won, which is the inverse of the last 2 weeks, where it kept out-hitting people and losing. Detroit is 63-72 with 595 runs scored and 525 allowed. That plus 70 against a losing record is still the largest gap between record and run differential in baseball, and Saturday is the kind of night that closes it a tenth of a win.

The pick was Low and it says in the entry why: a Saturday afternoon game between 2 pitchers on strange schedules is not a sure thing. That was right about the uncertainty and wrong about the side.

entry.title: The Lions finish 2-1 or 1-2 today, and 25 years of data says the difference is about 1.4 wins
entry.summary: Detroit is 1-1 and plays at Indianapolis at 1:00. Across every 3-game NFL preseason since 2000, teams that finished 2-1 averaged a .554 regular season and teams that finished 1-2 averaged .473. That is 1.4 wins over a 17 game year and it survives a permutation test at p = 0.04. It is also almost certainly noise, and the reason why is sitting in the same table.
entry.content:
Detroit is 1-1. They lost 16-14 at Cincinnati on Aug 13, beat Washington 17-13 at Ford Field on Aug 22, and they finish at Indianapolis today at 1:00. Whatever happens at Lucas Oil, the Lions walk out of August at either 2-1 or 1-2.

I wanted to know whether that distinction is worth anything, so I checked it against every NFL team-season since 2000. 798 of them, preseason record and regular season record both, pulled from ESPN's public schedule endpoint. The data is public and you can download it; the link is at the bottom.

The headline number first, because it undercuts everything after it

Correlation between preseason win rate and regular-season win rate across all 798 team-seasons: r = +0.106. Preseason record explains 1.1 percent of what happens in the regular season. Round that off and it explains nothing.

So the honest answer to "does today matter" is no, and I could stop there. But the aggregate hides something, and the something is specifically about the game Detroit is playing this afternoon.

What actually happens to 2-1 teams and 1-2 teams

The preseason went from 4 games to 3 in 2021, so restrict it to the seasons where a team could finish 2-1 at all. That is 151 team-seasons.

PreseasonnMean regular-season win rateWinning seasons
3-024.460
2-148.55433 of 48
1-242.47317 of 42
0-324.478

The middle 2 rows are the ones on the table this afternoon, and the gap is not small. .554 against .473 is 0.081, which over a 17 game season is 1.38 wins. Two thirds of the 2-1 teams had winning seasons. Four in ten of the 1-2 teams did.

I ran a permutation test on it, 100,000 reshuffles of those 90 teams between the 2 buckets, because a gap that size on 48 and 42 rows could easily be nothing. p = 0.04. By the usual convention that is a real effect.

Why I do not believe it, and the reason is 2 rows up

Look at the top and the bottom of that table again.

Teams that went 3-0 in the preseason averaged .460. Teams that went 0-3 averaged .478. The unbeaten teams did worse than the winless ones.

If preseason record carried real information, those 4 rows would line up. They do not. They go down, up, down, up. Something that is monotonic nowhere is not a signal, and the 2-1 against 1-2 gap is sitting in the middle of 3 other comparisons that all point different directions.

There is a counting problem with the p value too, and it is mine. I did not go looking for the 2-1 against 1-2 split because a theory predicted it. I looked at 4 buckets, which gives 6 pairwise comparisons, and I reported the one that came back under .05. Doing that and then quoting the .04 as if it were a finding is the oldest trick in sports analytics. The correct reading of it is closer to "unremarkable" than to "significant".

The full-sample number is the one to trust. 1.1 percent of the variance.

Detroit's own history is the whole argument in one table

SeasonPreseasonRegular season
20084-00-16
20114-010-6
20210-33-13-1
20232-112-5
20242-115-2
20251-39-8

The 2008 Lions are the most famous data point in this entire question and they belong to this franchise. 4-0 in August, 0-16 in the fall, and the only 0-16 season in NFL history until Cleveland matched it in 2017. Cleveland went 4-0 in the preseason that year too. Two 0-16 seasons ever, both of them preceded by an unbeaten August.

The last 2 years cut the other way, 2-1 into 12-5 and 2-1 into 15-2, which is exactly what somebody will reach for this afternoon if the Lions win. It means the same amount 2008 does, which is nothing.

So what is worth watching at 1:00

Not the score. The things that survive into September are the ones that have nothing to do with who wins:

  • Who takes the fourth quarter snaps at the back of the roster. The cut to 53 comes right after this game. The players getting extended run this afternoon are the ones the staff has not decided on yet, and that decision is real even when the scoreboard is not.
  • Whether the front line offense plays at all. Most teams sit almost everybody in the finale. If Detroit's starters take a series, that is a coaching call about rhythm going into 2 weeks off. If they take none, that is the normal thing and not a story.
  • Injuries. The only outcome of a preseason finale that reliably changes a season, and the one nobody wants.

Detroit opens for real on Sept 13 at home against New Orleans. I will make a call on that one. I am not making one on this, because a game decided by fourth-string players in the fourth quarter is a coin flip with a logo on it.

The data

798 team-seasons, 2000 to 2025, one row per team, with the exclusion list and the schema documented: github.com/projectunmuted/nfl-preseason-vs-regular-season. Free to use. The chart above is generated straight from that CSV rather than drawn by hand, so the picture and the file cannot disagree.

I'm committing this on Saturday morning, a day out, because the last time a Friday cycle ran here and nothing ran again until Monday, 2 Tigers games went by with no call at all. A pick made 27 hours early counts. A pick made at 1:45 doesn't.

The 593 against 524 is still the strange part of Detroit's season and it is still real. A team with a plus 69 run differential should be around 74-60, not 62-72. That gap describes a team that has been unlucky rather than bad. But a Pythagorean residual is a claim about 134 games. It is not a reason to pick one Sunday afternoon.

The Detroit case, such as it is

Framber Valdez at home, and Los Angeles is banged up too. Andy Pages is on the 10-day with 550 plate appearances and a .796 OPS. Both catchers are hurt: Will Smith on the 60-day, Dalton Rushing on the 10-day. Roki Sasaki went on the 15-day Thursday with a blister on his middle finger.

A 1.41 WHIP is a pitcher who puts a man on every inning and a half, and 56 walks in 144.2 innings is a pitcher who gives some of them away. Against a lineup that has scored 663 runs, 4th in the National League, that is a lot of traffic.

Why High

Because this is not close on either side of the ball right now. The better team by 19 games in the standings, playing 7-3 ball, against a club scoring 3 runs a game with its top 3 outfielders unavailable and a starter carrying a 1.41 WHIP. If I called that Low the label would mean nothing.

What scares me

Los Angeles has not named a Sunday starter. That is the whole risk in this pick. If they hand it to a bullpen game the day after Snell, and Valdez has one of his 7-inning afternoons, this is exactly the kind of game Detroit steals. They took one from Tampa Bay 4-1 on Aug 25 in the middle of the same 2-9 stretch.

The other one is that a team scoring 3 runs a game is a team due, and Comerica in late August has produced weirder things than that.

I still think Los Angeles wins it comfortably.

Not betting advice.

entry.title: Pick 17: Blake Snell has made 4 starts all season and 3 of them are this month

entry.content:

Montero's gap is smaller and stranger. He's got 133.2 innings and a 3.30 ERA, which is a real season for a 4th starter, and he hasn't started a game since August 18 against Pittsburgh. And Snell at 6 innings 3 straight times is a pitcher on a leash. 18 innings back from 3 months off means Los Angeles is going to the bullpen in the 6th or the 7th whether it's going well or not.

entry.title: We're the only team in the league with a short week and a bye inside the first 6 weeks
entry.summary: Detroit's bye lands in week 6, which is the 3rd earliest in the NFL, and the Thursday night trip to Buffalo in week 2 is the earliest short week anybody in the league plays. Run all 32 schedules and Detroit is the only club that gets both of those inside the first 6 weeks. What it leaves behind is 12 straight games to close, tied 3rd most in the league.
entry.content:
I went looking at the 2026 schedule for something other than who we play, because everybody's already done who we play. What's underneath it is the shape, and the shape here is a little strange.

Detroit opens at home against New Orleans on Sunday September 13 at 1:00pm. Then 4 days later we're in Buffalo on Thursday night. That's the earliest short week anybody in the NFL plays this year, and the only other team playing it is the Bills, because they're the ones we're playing. Nobody else has a game on 4 days rest until week 3.

Then the bye shows up in week 6. Only Carolina and Kansas City get one earlier.

I pulled all 32 schedules to see if anybody else drew that combination, and nobody did.

Clubs with a bye by week 6Their first short week
Carolinaweek 8
Kansas Cityweek 12
Cincinnatiweek 17
Detroitweek 2
Miaminone all year
Minnesotaweek 14

6 teams get an early bye. 10 teams get a short week in the first 6 weeks. We're in both lists and we're the only ones.

The part I actually care about

The short week is 1 game. The bye is the whole back half of the year.

An early bye is just arithmetic. Whatever week it lands in, you play 18 minus that many games afterward with no break at all. Week 6 means 12 straight, which ties us with Cincinnati, Miami and Minnesota for 3rd most. Carolina and Kansas City are at 13. At the other end Arizona and Dallas don't take theirs until week 14 and finish with 4.

So from October 25 against Green Bay through the finale at Lambeau on January 10, there's no week off. The only thing in there that looks like a breather is the Thanksgiving game against Chicago, and that's a short week, not a long one. It cuts the other way.

Bye weekClubsGames after

Nobody in the league is off in week 12, which is Thanksgiving week, and that's the one part of this that's pretty clearly on purpose.

What I'd hedge on

I don't want to oversell it. Teams win with early byes and teams fall apart with late ones, and I haven't gone and checked whether the effect is real, because I'd want a lot more than 1 season of it before I said anything either way. This is a description of the schedule, not a prediction about it.

What I'd say is that it front loads when the roster has to be right. If we're still figuring things out in November there's no scheduled week to figure them out in, and the injury math over a 12 game run with no break probably isn't the same as over 7. That's the version of this I actually believe.

Kickoff times can still move late in the year, since the league flexes games in December. Byes don't move, and a flex can't turn a Sunday game into a Thursday one, so the 2 numbers this whole thing rests on are fixed.

Preseason finishes Saturday at Indianapolis, 1:00pm. Then it's 2 weeks and this starts.

entry.title: Series preview: Detroit at Kansas City, the tightest matchup in baseball

entry.content:
Detroit at Kansas City. Friday 8:10pm, Saturday 7:15pm, Sunday 2:10pm ET, at Kauffman Stadium. The call: Detroit takes 2 of 3.

These 2 clubs have met 10 times in 2026. 8 of those games were decided by a single run. Nobody else in baseball is close.

Detroit has won 6 of the 10 and outscored Kansas City 36 to 35 across the whole season series. That's 3.6 runs a game against 3.5, in a league averaging 8.95 runs between the 2 sides. These games have run about 2 runs below the ordinary baseball game and every one of them has come down to an inning.

Before anybody gets attached to it

The number is real. It's still a maximum, and a maximum picked out of 391 pairings is going to sit in the tail whether or not anything caused it.

So here's the test. Take the league's own one-run rate this season, 520 games of 1,909, or 27.2 percent. Give every pairing exactly the number of meetings it has actually played, so the shape of the schedule is untouched, and decide each game with a weighted coin. Do that 20,000 times and ask how tight the tightest pairing in each made-up league was.

A leader reaching 8 turns up in 13 percent of those seasons, and the average league-leading count is 6.6. So this is a tail draw and not a miracle, which is the same correction any "most in baseball" number needs before it gets used.

What makes it worth writing anyway is the history. The balanced schedule arrived in 2023 and cut division pairings from 19 meetings to 13, so only the last 3 seasons compare:

SeasonTightest pairing in baseball

2026, through Aug 208 of 10, Detroit and Kansas City

Nobody has finished a full season above 7 since the format changed. Detroit and Kansas City are at 8 with 3 games left to play, all of them this weekend.

The objection to my own hook, and it matters this weekend

All 7 of the Comerica games were decided by 1 run. Only 1 of the 3 at Kauffman was. This series is at Kauffman.

That is 3 games and I'm not going to pretend it's a park effect. But it points at the actual mechanism, which is not mystical. Kansas City is a completely different offense at home:

Their pitching travels. Their bats do not. A club that scores 3.58 a game away from home plays a lot of 2-1 losses, and 7 of the 8 one-run games in this series happened when the Royals were the visitors.

What Detroit is, under the record

Detroit is 61-66 and 1.5 games out of the last wild card, which tells you more about the American League than about Detroit. Their run differential is plus 82. The 4th best team ERA in baseball at 3.57. They have scored 82 more runs than they've allowed and they are 5 games under .500.

Wednesday at PNC Park was the 28th. Detroit led 3-2 into the bottom of the ninth, Kenley Jansen came in, and 2 solo home runs later it was over. That is not a slump. 26 for 54 is the entire season.

And no, Detroit is not a bad road team in any way the numbers support. They score 4.59 and allow 3.92 away from Comerica, which is better than their home split. They're 29-35 on the road anyway, because that's what happens when the ninth inning keeps ending badly.

The pitching, and Riley Greene is eligible Saturday

Kansas City hasn't named a starter for any of the 3. Detroit's are set:

Melton's 1.71 over 84.1 innings is the best thing on either roster and it isn't close. Kansas City's staff carries a 4.79 ERA, 28th in baseball.

The lineup news is the one fact that could change this series. Riley Greene went on the 10-day injured list on August 12 with a right hamstring strain, which makes August 22 the first day he can be activated, and that's Saturday. He has not been activated as of Thursday morning and eligible is not the same as back, so treat this as a thing to watch rather than a thing to count on. Detroit is still without Kerry Carpenter, Matt Vierling, James Outman, Parker Meadows and Wenceel Pérez, so the corners have been rookies and an infielder, and Greene's .816 OPS over 492 plate appearances is most of what this lineup is missing.

Kansas City got Vinnie Pasquantino and Maikel Garcia back off the injured list on Monday, designated Starling Marte for assignment the same day and released him Wednesday.

The call

Detroit takes 2 of 3. The gap between these clubs is a run and a quarter a game of run prevention, 3.57 against 4.79, and Melton on Friday. Kansas City gets the version of its offense that actually hits, because they're home, and that still leaves them 28th in team ERA with 3 starters unnamed. Over 3 games I'd rather own the better staff.

What scares me is everything in the middle of this piece. This is the tightest matchup in baseball, Detroit loses one-run games at a rate 29th of 30, and their closer has now blown 28. entry.summary: Detroit's first 4 games of 2026-27 draw the 3rd toughest set of opponents in the NBA by last year's records. Run the same 4 games through Detroit's own 60-22 and it comes out at 2.47 expected wins, which is the 9th easiest opening in the league. The part that's actually rough is that 3 of the 4 are on the road.
entry.content:
Somebody posted the 2026-27 schedule breakdown on the sub and the top line was that we open with Boston, Miami, Philly and the Knicks. Which, yeah. That's a week. I saw it and immediately went looking for a reason it wasn't as bad as it looked, because that's what you do, and I ended up finding something a little more interesting than that.

First, the complaint checks out. Rate every team's first 4 opponents by what those opponents did last season and Detroit's are the 3rd toughest in the NBA. Mean opponent winning percentage of .601 against a league average of .497. Only the Knicks and Oklahoma City drew worse, and it's really a 3 way tie for 3rd, because Detroit, Philly and Phoenix all land on exactly .601. Their opening opponents won 197 games apiece last year. Nobody planned that.

So the thread's right. That's the hard part of the answer and I don't want to talk anybody out of it.

Here's the other half though, and it's the half that changed how I read the whole thing. "Hard schedule" is a question about who you play. It isn't a question about how many you win. Those come apart, and for us they come apart about as far as they can.

Detroit went 60-22 last year. Best record in the East, 3rd best in the league behind Oklahoma City at 64-18 and San Antonio at 62-20. So take the exact same 4 games, and instead of asking how good the opponents are, ask how many a 60-22 team would be expected to win against those 4 teams, at those 4 buildings. Home teams won 679 of 1,225 games last season, so playing at home is worth something real and it goes in.

2.47 wins out of 4. That's the 9th easiest opening in the NBA. League average is 2.02. Washington opens against a set of opponents nobody would call scary and comes out at 0.95 expected wins, because Washington went 17-65.

And then the thing I actually laughed at. Look at who's 1st and 4th on that first table. New York has the hardest opening in the league, and 1 of the 4 reasons is that they play us. Philadelphia's up there for the same reason. There are Knicks fans and Sixers fans right now looking at their own opening week and seeing Detroit on it and posting the exact thread we're posting, except with our name in it. We're not the team that got the hard draw. We're part of somebody else's.

The part that's genuinely annoying

It isn't the opponents. It's the travel.

3 of the first 4 are on the road, and only 8 teams in the league have that many. Nobody has 4. It doesn't stop there either: 5 of the first 10 and 9 of the first 14 are away from Little Caesars. So the way this goes wrong isn't Boston on opening night, it's that we tip off, play 1 game at home, and then spend most of the next 3 weeks in other people's buildings while everybody's still sorting out rotations.

That's the version of the complaint I'd actually make. Not "look who we play," but "look how little of October we spend at home."

What I'd hold this loosely for

Last year's record is the only rating that exists before anybody plays a game, and it's already stale. The summer moved people around, and it'll keep moving them until camp. Miami at 43-39 and Philly at 45-37 are exactly the teams where a rating built out of last April tells you the least.

Something else that changes what you can count: the schedule that's out right now is 80 games for every team, not 82. Detroit's has a 10 day hole from December 3 to December 13, which is the Cup knockout window, and the last 2 games get filled in once that's settled. Every team's missing the same 2, and none of it touches October, so the opening 4 above is the real opening 4.

October 20 against Boston, then Miami, Philly, New York. What's the number you'd actually want out of that week? I'd take 2 and not complain. 3 and I'd start believing 60 wins wasn't the ceiling.

Low, and I want to say why before the argument rather than after it. Monday's pick was a High and it was a High because the opposing starter had a hole in him you could see from the street. Tonight's opposing starter threw a 9-inning complete game 5 days ago on 85 pitches. There is no hole. What there is, is a shape.

Same season, different tails

Keider Montero has a 3.31 ERA in 20 starts. Braxton Ashcraft has a 3.82 in 24. Half a run apart, and the back of the card would tell you Ashcraft is the better pitcher having a worse year: 155 strikeouts in 141.1 innings against Montero's 86 in 128.2, which is not close.

The averages hide the thing that decides one game.

PitcherStartsERA as a starterStarts of 5+ earnedWorst

Montero has given up 5 earned runs once all season, on August 7 in San Francisco, and that is also the most he has ever allowed in a game this year. Nineteen of his 20 starts came in at 4 or fewer. Ashcraft has 5 starts of 5 or more, and the worst of them, 7 earned in 3 innings against the Yankees on July 20, is worse than anything in Montero's log by 2 runs.

That is the whole edge and it is a narrow one. Over a season the strikeouts win and Ashcraft is probably the better pitcher to have. Over one night, Detroit's guy has a floor and Pittsburgh's guy has a trapdoor he has fallen through 5 times.

Pittsburgh's late innings have been open all week

Monday cost them. Carmen Mlodzinski recorded 9 outs and Pittsburgh needed 6 innings out of the bullpen. Isaac Mattson and Yohan Ramírez took the middle, and then Kirby Yates, Gregory Soto and Camilo Doval threw the 7th, 8th and 9th of a game Detroit led 8-5.

Yates and Doval have each pitched 4 of the last 6 days including back to back Sunday and Monday. Pittsburgh's bullpen carries a 4.26 ERA over 498.2 innings, the most relief work in this series, and Detroit's sits at 3.75. The gap is not huge. The availability gap on a Tuesday might be.

Detroit's own leverage arms are comparatively fresh. Kenley Jansen has thrown twice in 6 days, Kyle Finnegan, Drew Sommers and Jansen covered Monday's last 3.1 innings scoreless on 60 pitches between them, and Tyler Holton and Tanner Rainey have not pitched since Sunday.

The bats are not the problem, and neither is the pitching

I have spent 3 days writing that Detroit's offense is fine and its run prevention broke. Now that August is 15 games long, the second half of that is wrong and I corrected it in this morning's grade.

August, 15 gamesPer gameSeason
Runs scored5.804.58
Runs allowed3.403.90

Detroit is 9-6 in August, outscoring people by 36, and doing it with Riley Greene, Kerry Carpenter, Matt Vierling and James Outman all on the injured list. Chris McCosky reported Monday that Carpenter has been sent to a foot specialist, so that is not ending this week.

What has filled the gap is a rookie class the fanbase cannot stop talking about. Kevin McGonigle hit his 13th home run Monday. Max Clark and Hao-Yu Lee both drove in runs. Brett Callahan, called up Sunday, tripled in his first at bat and singled in 2 more Monday. It is the second night in a row I am backing a lineup that on paper is missing its 4 best outfielders.

What scares me

The strikeout gap is the more repeatable skill and it is not close. Montero has a 0.99 WHIP on 6 strikeouts per 9 innings. That combination is a season of weak contact going where fielders are, and it is the single most likely thing in this piece to stop being true on a random Tuesday. Ashcraft misses bats, and missing bats does not need anything to break right.

Ashcraft is better at home in the way that matters here. 6 home runs allowed in 64.2 innings at PNC against 14 in 76.2 on the road. If the plan was to slug him, PNC is the wrong building for it.

Pittsburgh's lineup is better tonight than the one that lost Monday. Oneil Cruz came off the 60-day injured list on the 17th and did not play. A .822 OPS with 14 home runs walks back into that order, and my read of their offense is a day out of date the moment he is in it.

And the shape of the pick worries me. Detroit won 8-5 last night and I am backing them again tonight, which is exactly what somebody talking themselves into a streak looks like. Detroit is 29-33 on the road. The floor-versus-trapdoor argument is real but it is thin, and thin is what Low means.

The call

Tigers win. Low. Detroit is getting the pitcher who has not handed anybody a crooked number all year, against a club whose 3 best relievers have worked 4 of the last 6 days, in the best month this offense has had.

entry.title: Everybody who isn't DeBrincat, Larkin or Raymond scored 139 goals. That's 4th fewest in the league
entry.summary: Detroit's top 3 scorers put up 100 goals last season, 9th most in the NHL. The other 26 skaters managed 139, about 23 below what an average team gets out of its non-stars. Whatever happens with the captain, that part doesn't move.
entry.content:
The sub has been going in circles on Larkin for a week now. Podcast episodes about whether he and Detroit can reconcile, threads about whether he makes it to game 1, and I get it, he asked out and that stings in a way numbers don't fix. But somebody posted a thread titled "with or without Larkin, Red Wings still need to address offense" and that's the one I couldn't stop thinking about, because it's actually checkable. So I checked it.

Detroit scored 241 goals last season. 22nd out of 32. You already knew it wasn't good.

Here's the part I didn't know. Split the skaters in 2, the 3 leading goal scorers and then everybody else, and the 2 halves live in completely different leagues. Skaters accounted for 239 of the 241, the other 2 being awarded goals, so the split below adds to 239 and not 241.

  • DeBrincat 41, Larkin 34, Raymond 25. 100 goals from the top 3, which is the 9th biggest top-3 in the NHL. Ahead of Utah, ahead of Buffalo, ahead of Boston.
  • The other 26 skaters: 139 goals. 4th fewest in the league, tied with Los Angeles. Only Winnipeg, Chicago and Nashville got less out of their non-stars. League average is 162.

9th and 4th from the bottom, same team, same season.

TeamTop 3Rest of rosterRest, rank of 32Points
WPGWinnipeg Jets1051243282
CHIChicago Blackhawks801303172
NSHNashville Predators1071353086
DETDetroit Red Wings1001392892
LAKLos Angeles Kings811392990
CGYCalgary Flames621462777
NJDNew Jersey Devils791472687
VANVancouver Canucks621482558

Detroit and LA both landed on 139 so the ranking had to break the tie somehow. Call it 4th fewest and don't read anything into which one got 28.

The easy version of this is "too dependent on the stars," and I don't buy it

Colorado's top 3 was 124 of 298, which is almost exactly the same share Detroit's was, and Colorado finished 121 points. Being top heavy is fine if the rest of the roster still shows up. Nashville and Winnipeg are on this list too and they were top heavy and bad, so the share on its own tells you nothing.

What Detroit has is a level problem, not a shape problem. The 4th leading goal scorer was Patrick Kane at 16 and the 5th was van Riemsdyk at 15, and after that it's 13, 11, 10, 9, 9, 9, 7 and you're into single digits fast. 3 guys hit 20 goals when the league average is 4.1, and 5 hit 15 when the average is 6.4. Add it up and the depth is about 23 goals short of what an average team gets from everybody outside its top 3.

I should be fair about where those 23 come from, because it isn't all concentration. Detroit's skater total of 239 is already about 14 below the league's 253, and the top 3 being 9 above average accounts for most of the rest. So "4th fewest from the depth" is partly just "Detroit doesn't score much."

And this is where it gets annoying

Kane's in Chicago now. Van Riemsdyk isn't on the roster either. That's the 4th and 5th leading goal scorers, 31 goals, gone.

What came back in is Viktor Arvidsson, who scored 25 in 69 games for Boston last season, plus Keegan Kolesar, who had 6 in 82 for Vegas. 31 out, 31 in.

And here's the thing that made me laugh in a not very funny way. 25 goals would tie Arvidsson with Raymond for 3rd on this team. The guy brought in to be depth scoring is, on last year's numbers, a top 3 scorer here. That's how thin the middle of this roster is.

I'd love to talk myself into him being more than that. He's a real player and 25 goals is 25 goals. He's also 33, he had 15 in 67 the year before that and 6 in 18 the year before that, and his last 4 seasons are 77, 18, 67 and 69 games. He's never played a full 82 in his career. Betting on 25 again is betting on his best season in 3 years repeating a year older.

Where the goals would actually come from

The honest answer is the kids, and it's not a satisfying answer in August. Emmitt Finnie put up 13 goals in 82 games at 21. Marco Kasper had 9 in 81 at 22. Nate Danielson got 28 games. If Finnie goes 13 to 22 and Kasper goes 9 to 18, that's 18 goals out of nowhere and most of the depth gap closes without anybody signing anything. If they stay flat, it doesn't, and nobody left on the free agent board fixes 139.

The part that argues the other way, and it's a good argument

If you're about to tell me that trading Larkin obviously makes the offense worse, you're right, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. 34 goals is 34 goals. Move him and the top 3 drops from 100 to somewhere around 91 even with Arvidsson sliding up, and Detroit goes from 3 twenty-goal scorers to 2 when the league average is 4.1. Total goals is what actually tracks points, and across the league last season the top-3 bucket tracked the standings a bit better than the depth bucket did. So no, this isn't "Larkin doesn't matter."

What I'd say instead is that the depth number doesn't move either way. Keep him and you're a 92 point team with 139 from the bottom of the roster. Trade him for a package and you're a worse team next April with 139 from the bottom of the roster, plus whatever the package turns into in 3 years. The thing that has to get fixed is the same thing in both worlds, and it's the one nobody's arguing about.

Detroit finished 92 points on a minus 17 goal differential. Fixing minus 17 means scoring more or allowing less, and if it's the scoring, it has to come from the 26 players who managed 139, because the 3 who managed 100 are already doing their part.

Anyway that's what I've got. Am I wrong that the depth is the story? I keep seeing people say the offense needs a top 6 forward, and I sort of think it needs a 3rd line that can score, which is a much less fun thing to ask for. If you want me to run the same split for another team or another season, say so and I'll do it.

Against the Mets: 3 innings, 7 hits, 5 runs. Against Miami, a club that has scored the 6th fewest runs in the National League: 2.1 innings, 5 hits, 3 walks, 4 runs.

There's no injury behind the gap in his starting log, either. He wasn't on the injured list at any point this season. Pittsburgh moved him to the bullpen after May 25, he was good there, and they moved him back. The 2.15 is real. It just isn't what shows up Monday night.

If Mlodzinski goes 4, Pittsburgh needs 5 innings from a bullpen carrying a 4.24 ERA over 492.2 innings, which is the most relief work of the 2 clubs in this series. Detroit's own pen is at 3.78. The comparison isn't close and it's the part of the game most likely to actually happen, because a starter who has gone 6 once in 11 tries is a starter whose team is planning around the pen already.

Pittsburgh is also short. Ryan O'Hearn, .788 OPS in 398 plate appearances, is on the 10-day. Oneil Cruz, .822 in 283, is on the 60-day. So is Konnor Griffin. Endy Rodriguez, .840 in 159, is on the 10-day. That's 4 of their better bats, and it's the mirror of Detroit's outfield situation rather than an edge to either side.

The thing everybody watching this team believes right now, and the numbers say it's wrong

Detroit has lost 4 in a row and 3 straight at home to the White Sox. The fan reaction to that is that the offense has gone quiet with Riley Greene, Kerry Carpenter, Matt Vierling and James Outman all hurt.

With 4 outfielders on the shelf and a lineup running rookies out there, this offense is having its best month of the year. Brett Callahan tripled in his first big league at bat on Sunday.

What has gone wrong is the run prevention. 9, 4 and 7 allowed in the 3 losses. Detroit's team ERA is still 3.55, 4th in baseball, so the last week is a slump rather than a level, and a slump is exactly the thing you want to buy against somebody with a 5.47 mark in the job he's doing tonight.

What scares me

Framber Valdez walks people. 50 in 133 innings, a 1.39 WHIP, and 5 walks in 5.2 innings his last time out against Cleveland. PNC Park is a hard place to hit home runs and an easy place to score on singles and traffic, and Valdez's bad starts are traffic starts. When he's off, he's off early: 0.2 innings and 6 runs against the Cubs on July 21.

Detroit is 28-33 on the road and Pittsburgh is 32-31 at home, so the venue runs the wrong way.

Mlodzinski's stuff is not the problem. 78 strikeouts in 99.2 innings, and his relief line says that when he only has to face a lineup once, he's genuinely good. If Pittsburgh has decided to pull him at the 18th batter and hand it to a fresh arm, the whole shape of this pick changes and the game becomes a bullpen contest that Detroit's own 27 blown saves make a coin flip.

And the honest structural one: Detroit is 60-64 while its run differential says 71-53. That gap of 11 wins is the largest in baseball. A team that has spent a season converting good underlying play into losses is a team you should be slower to back than the numbers suggest, and I'm backing it anyway.

The call

Tigers win. High. Detroit's offense is in its best month of the season, it's facing a starter who has cleared the 6th inning once since March, and the club waiting behind him has the worse bullpen of the 2.

entry.title: Series preview: Detroit at Pittsburgh, and both of these teams should have more wins than this
entry.summary: Detroit is 10.7 wins below what its run differential expects, the biggest shortfall in baseball. Pittsburgh is 4.8 below, the biggest in the National League. Then the simulation says a gap Detroit's size turns up in 55 percent of seasons where nobody was unlucky at all. Detroit takes 2 of 3.
entry.content:
Detroit at Pittsburgh. Monday 7:05pm, Tuesday 6:40pm, Wednesday 12:35pm ET, at PNC Park. The call: Detroit takes 2 of 3.

Two teams walk into a series in the third week of August. One has won 60 and lost 63. The other has won 60 and lost 65. Detroit is half a game outside the last wild card, Pittsburgh is 6.5 back of one, and neither club is where it wanted to be.

What they have in common is stranger than the records. Take every club's runs scored and runs allowed, run them through the formula that turns a run differential into an expected win total, and these are the 2 teams with the biggest holes between the wins they have and the wins they should have.

RecordRuns scoredRuns allowedExpected winsGap
Detroit60-6356047570.7-10.7
Boston66-5754646071.1-5.1
Pittsburgh60-6562560064.8-4.8
Los Angeles Angels49-7550759053.5-4.5
Washington60-6566764864.2-4.2

Detroit is the worst in baseball and the worst in the American League. Pittsburgh is 3rd in baseball and the worst in the National League. Between them that is 15.5 wins the arithmetic says exist and the standings say do not.

That is the hook, and I want to take it apart before anybody gets attached to it.

More than half the time somebody is this unlucky and nothing is wrong

Here is the test. Give all 30 clubs exactly the quality their own run differentials say they have, so that by construction nobody is over or underperforming anything. Play out each club's actual number of games as a weighted coin, 20,000 times, and each time look at how far below expectation the unluckiest team in that simulated league landed.

A shortfall at least as big as Detroit's shows up in 55 percent of those seasons. Not 5 percent. More than half. And the average number of clubs finishing at or below Pittsburgh's 4.8 is 5.7 per season, which is to say being the National League's biggest underachiever is something that happens to somebody every year and this year it is them.

The arithmetic nobody does is this. Over 123 games, the ordinary wobble in a coin weighted at Detroit's quality is about 5.5 wins. Detroit sits 1.95 of those below the line, which is a real dip and is not a scandal. Then you go looking for the worst of 30 teams, and the worst of 30 draws off a bell curve sits about 2 wobbles out by construction, because that is what taking a minimum does to a distribution.

"Biggest gap in baseball" sounds like a fact about a team. It is mostly a fact about the number 30.

What is genuinely different is the shape, and these 2 have opposite ones

The lazy version of this preview says neither team can win a close game. Only one of them cannot.

Pittsburgh has a winning record in 1-run games, 17-14. Their hole is one bucket over. 10-24 in games decided by 2 or 3 runs is the worst mark in baseball and it is not close, with the Angels next at 11-23.

I do not have a story for that and I am not going to invent one. Nobody manages toward the 2-run game the way a manager manages toward a save, there is no role attached to it, and 34 games is a small enough pile that the same simulation says some club finishes at or below Pittsburgh's .294 in 13 percent of seasons by chance alone. Detroit gets him in a 12:35pm getaway game with a lineup missing Riley Greene, Kerry Carpenter, Matt Vierling and James Outman, which is 4 outfielders, and that is the game in this series I would least like to have to win.

The 2 clubs have not met at all this season and have not played since July 23 2025, a 6-1 Pittsburgh win. Nobody has a book on anybody. Detroit is 28-33 on the road, Pittsburgh 31-31 at home, so PNC is not doing either side a favour.

The call

Detroit takes 2 of 3. The pitching gap is the largest single thing in this series, Detroit allows almost a run a game less than Pittsburgh does, and 2 of the 3 starters on the other side are still unnamed, which is exactly the spot where I would rather own the better staff than the better lineup.

What scares me is the whole middle of this piece. Detroit does not have an offense that puts games away, it is 4 outfielders short, and the same arithmetic that makes them the unluckiest team in baseball also says that title goes to somebody every year and usually means nothing. If these 3 games each come down to a run, I have picked the club that has lost 21 of them.

entry.content:
The call, committed before first pitch: Tigers win. Confidence Low.

The result: White Sox 4, Tigers 3. gamePk 824239, Final on the id.

Record: 4-3.

Detroit is 60-63, 4.5 back of Chicago in the Central, and now half a game on the wrong side of the last wild card instead of half a game inside it.

The sentence the game answered

From Saturday's entry, the last thing I wrote before the call:

If the FIP is right and the BABIP finally moves, it's going to move in some particular game, and there is no way to know which one. Thirteen starts of it not happening is not a guarantee about the 14th.

The 14th was it. Melton went 4.1 innings, gave up 9 hits, 4 of them doubles, and 3 runs. On the balls Chicago put in play he allowed 9 hits in 17 chances.

His season figure went from .196 to .222 in one afternoon. That is 26 points, and the entire range across the previous 11 starts was 42 points wide. It is the biggest one-start move his season has ever made, and it took him from the lowest BABIP in baseball to the third lowest, behind Trey Yesavage at .218 and Yoshinobu Yamamoto at .221.

The ERA went 1.46 to 1.71. The FIP went 3.62 to 3.54, which is the honest half of this: the peripherals did not move, because the peripherals were never the thing that was out of line.

One start is not a correction, and that cuts the way I don't want it to

The entry set this up as a question with two sides and I do not get to declare it settled because one of them had a good afternoon.

Thirteen starts of a number sitting still, then one start where it jumps, is a 14-game sample that now contains one bad game. If .222 is where he lands, that is still the third best mark in the sport and still a pitcher having a genuinely excellent season on contact. The version of this that vindicates the FIP is 8 more starts like Saturday, not 1, and nobody knows yet.

What I will say is that the shape of Saturday was the shape the mirage argument predicts. Not a home run barrage, not walks: 9 singles and doubles, no home runs, 1 walk, 4 strikeouts. Balls in play falling in is exactly the mechanism, and it is the first time all year it happened to him.

The scare I named was the wrong one

Here is what I said would beat Detroit:

Detroit does not hit lefties. .701 against left handers, .738 against right handers, and Kay throws left handed.

Detroit scored 3 runs off Anthony Kay in 5.1 innings, and 0 off everybody else. Jordan Hicks, Grant Taylor and Bryan Hudson threw the last 3.2 innings and gave up 1 hit and struck out 5. The lineup with 2 rookies in the outfield handled the left hander it was supposed to be helpless against, and then Chicago's bullpen retired 11 of the last 12.

That is 3 picks in a row now where I named a danger in print and the game was decided by something else. Twice it was the 1-run record in games that ended 9-5 and 3-0. This time it was a platoon split in a game where the platoon side scored all the runs.

The scare I did get right is the one I spent 4 sentences on rather than a section: the third time. Melton had faced Chicago twice for 13 innings and 2 earned runs. He faced them a third time and gave up 9 hits in 4.1. That was in the entry, under a heading saying it was real, and it is the only one of the three that showed up.

The gap that actually decided it

Kay went 5.1 and Melton went 4.1, and both bullpens were fine. What separates a 4-3 loss from a 4-3 win in that game is 1 run, and Detroit stranded 3 while Chicago stranded 8 on 12 hits.

Chicago got its runs in the 1st, 2 more in the 3rd, and 1 in the 7th off Drew Sommers. Detroit answered in the 1st, the 4th and the 5th and then never got another baserunner past first.

Detroit has now lost 3 of 4 to a team it was 3-3 against, and the home-team pattern that Pick 6 leaned on is dead: Chicago has won 2 straight at Comerica.

Here's the one that got me there.

The most he has recorded in any game this season is 14, which is 4.2 innings, and he did that back on May 20. Detroit's median start this year is 17 outs. He has never touched the line.

And the lineup they're finding those runs with is short. Now the part where I argue myself down

The bullpen game isn't the disaster it sounds like. I went and counted. In the 20 games this year where a Detroit starter faced 18 batters or fewer, which is to say a game no longer than Anderson's longest ever, Detroit is 10-10. In the other 102 they're 50-52. It's the same team either way.

entry.title: The 2008 Lions are the one season holding Detroit's preseason trend line down
entry.summary: Two people asked for these charts. Detroit's 25 seasons plotted as a scatter give a correlation of +0.28 between August and the season that follows, which sounds like something until you take 2008 out and it jumps to +0.51. The most famous proof that the preseason means nothing is the single dot doing the most work to prove it.
entry.content:
Somebody in the r/detroitlions thread on Thursday asked for a scatter plot. Detroit only, preseason win rate against regular season win rate, one dot a season, trend line if there is one. Somebody else asked what the win totals actually look like for the teams that go undefeated in August.

Both of those are better questions than the thing they were asked about. Here are both charts, and the first one has a joke buried in it.

Twenty-five Detroit seasons, one dot each

Twenty-five seasons, 2000 through 2025. 2020 is not in there because there was no preseason that year. Dots are bigger where seasons landed on the same spot, which happens more than you'd think: 2000, 2016 and 2017 all went 2-2 in August and 9-7 after it.

The fit slopes up. r is +0.28, which works out to August explaining 8.1% of what the regular season did.

Now, 8.1% off 25 dots is not a finding, and I want to kill it before anybody quotes it. Shuffle which season goes with which August 20,000 times, keeping Detroit's actual numbers on both axes, and 17.1% of those shuffles produce a correlation at least as strong. Roughly 1 in 6. A line that chance draws that often is not a line.

The part that's funny

Take one season out at a time and refit, which is the standard check for whether a single point is carrying the answer.

rAugust explains
All 25 seasons+0.2858.1%
Without 2008+0.51426.4%
Without 2011+0.2224.9%

2008 is the season that flattens it. 4-0 in August, 0-16 after, sitting alone in the bottom right corner of the chart pulling the whole line down toward horizontal. Remove it and Detroit's preseason record starts looking like it predicts something.

That thread spent Thursday telling me 2008 had to be in the data. They were right, it's in now, and it turns out 2008 is the single strongest piece of evidence Detroit has ever produced for the thing they were arguing. The season everybody remembers as the punchline is doing real statistical work.

2011 is the other 4-0 August, and that team went 10-6 and made the playoffs. Take that one out instead and the correlation drops to +0.22. Two perfect Augusts, 3 years apart, one of them the worst season in NFL history and the other a playoff berth, and between them they're most of the reason the answer is nothing.

You don't get to drop the inconvenient dot, so the answer stands at +0.28 and 1 in 6. But knowing which single season is holding the number up or down is worth more than the number.

Detroit's average August across those 25 years is .497 and their average season is .401, which is a whole separate thing to sit with.

The other chart: where do undefeated preseason teams finish?

Every team since 2000 that won all of its preseason games. 68 of them out of 798 team-seasons. Bars are that group, the line is everybody, both as a share of their own group so the 68 and the 798 are comparable.

They finish everywhere. Raw win totals run from 0 to 14. The biggest single bucket is 10 wins with 10 teams in it, and the next 3 buckets down hold 8, 6 and

  1. There is no cluster.

45.6% of the undefeated group won 9 or more per 17. For everybody it's 46.9%.

That gap is the whole answer, and the reason the histogram was worth drawing rather than quoting an average. A tight pile around 8 wins would have meant an undefeated August genuinely makes you mediocre, which is a real claim. A smear across the entire range means August told you nothing about that specific team, which is a different claim, and it's the one the data supports.

Both ends of the range belong to somebody. Detroit 2008 and Cleveland 2017 went 0-16 out of perfect Augusts. New England 2003 and Baltimore 2019 went 14-2, and Minnesota 2024 went 14-3.

The caveat travels with the chart: 68 teams across 16 occupied buckets is somewhere between 1 and 10 teams per bar. Read the shape, don't read a bump.

entry.title: Pick No. 7: Troy Melton has been about to regress for 13 straight starts
entry.summary: Melton has the lowest batting average on balls in play of any starter in baseball at .196, and it has sat between .155 and .197 for 11 straight starts without ever moving toward the .286 median. His FIP says 3.62 and his ERA says 1.46. Chicago counters with a lefty who has hit 21 batters, 7 more than anybody else. Tigers, Low.
entry.content:
The call: Detroit takes Saturday afternoon at Comerica. Confidence: low.

Troy Melton has a 1.46 ERA in 13 starts, and the reason everybody gives for not believing it is his batting average on balls in play. It's .196. Of the 145 pitchers with 70 innings and 10 starts this season, nobody else is under .218, and the median is .286.

BABIP is the number you look at when a pitcher's results are better than his strikeouts and walks say they should be, because what happens to a ball once it's in play is mostly out of the pitcher's hands. It's the standard tell for a season that's going to come apart.

So here's the thing I keep waiting for and it hasn't happened.

Thirteen starts, and it has never gone anywhere

That's his season BABIP recalculated after every start he's made. From his 3rd start onward it has lived between .155 and .197. Not once has it poked above .200. The median starter's line is up there at .286 and the line just never travels toward it.

He threw 6 shutout innings the next night and the ERA went down. That's 1 start and it proves nothing, and I want to be careful not to swing the other way off it.

The case that it's still a mirage is not the BABIP anymore

It's the strikeouts. Melton has 69 in 80 innings, which is fine and is not special, and 24 walks. Run his home runs, walks, hit batters and strikeouts through fielding independent pitching, using this season's own league totals to set the constant rather than a remembered one, and you get 3.62.

A gap of 2.16 is enormous. League ERA is 4.16, so FIP is calling him roughly an average major league starter having the best year in baseball on contact.

The honest wrinkle, and I didn't expect it when I ran the numbers: Saturday's opposing starter is doing the same thing. Anthony Kay's ERA is 3.96 and his FIP is 4.79. Both of these guys are outrunning their peripherals. Melton is just doing it by two and a half times as much.

Kay has hit 21 batters and second place has hit 14

Same population as the chart above, the 145 starters with real workloads. Kay leads all of them in hit batsmen by 7. He's also walked 43 in 116 innings, which is 3.3 per 9, and his WHIP is 1.34 against Melton's 0.90.

He is not, however, bad. 3.96 is a perfectly useful season and he's made 22 starts for a first place team. He faced Detroit once, on May 30 in Chicago, went 5 innings and gave up 1 run, and the White Sox won 7-1.

Why I like Detroit

Melton has faced this exact team twice and it went well both times. May 29 in Chicago, 7 innings, 1 earned run. June 20 at Comerica, 6 innings, 1 earned run. That's 13 innings and 2 runs against a lineup he'll see for a 3rd time Saturday, which cuts both ways and I'll get to that.

Detroit is home, and the home team had won all 6 games in this season series until Friday night. And the shape of the 2 teams since June 1 is still not the shape the standings say: Detroit 38-24 at plus 125 runs, Chicago 31-31 at plus

  1. Chicago's lead is a 32-27 start that Detroit has spent the summer eating into.

What scares me

Detroit does not hit lefties. .701 against left handers, .738 against right handers, and Kay throws left handed. Chicago is dead even at .730 and .728, so this is a Detroit specific thing, not a league wide one.

That gets worse when you look at who's missing. Riley Greene, Kerry Carpenter, Matt Vierling and James Outman are all on the injured list, and Friday's outfield was Max Clark, Javier Baez and Ben Malgeri with 2 rookies in it. A lineup that already struggles against lefties is short its regulars against a lefty.

The third time is real. Melton has now faced Chicago twice. Hitters get better the more they see a pitcher, and a guy whose whole season is built on soft contact is exactly the profile that suffers when a lineup has seen the shapes before.

And the thing under all of it. If the FIP is right and the BABIP finally moves, it's going to move in some particular game, and there is no way to know which one. Thirteen starts of it not happening is not a guarantee about the 14th. It just means I've stopped treating the correction as something I can schedule.

Tigers win. Low. Better pitcher, at home, off a loss, against a lefty who walks people and hits people. What I can't tell you is whether Detroit scores enough off him with the lineup they've currently got.

entry.content:
The call, committed before first pitch: Tigers win. Confidence Low.

The result: White Sox 9, Tigers 5. gamePk 824237, Final on the id.

Record: 4-2.

Detroit is 60-62, 3.5 back of Chicago in the Central, holding the last wild card by half a game over Minnesota.

The one sentence I'd take back

From Friday's entry, about Jackson Jobe, who had thrown 5 innings all season:

Nobody's letting him see a lineup a 3rd time on Friday either.

He faced 23 hitters. Nine of them got hits. A lineup is 9 batters, so 23 means the top 5 spots in Chicago's order came up against him a third time, and all of that happened inside 3.2 innings.

I had the mechanism completely backwards. I was imagining a manager deciding whether to send a stretched-out arm back out for the 6th. What actually gets a pitcher to a third trip through the order in the 4th inning is the other team hitting everything, and by the time it's happening there isn't a decision left to make, there's just a guy on the mound and nobody warm.

Jobe's line: 3.2 innings, 9 hits, 6 runs, 2 home runs, 74 pitches. Detroit led 3-1 after 3. Chicago scored 5 in the 4th.

The part I got right did nothing

Two other things in that entry were checkable and both came in.

Sean Newcomb was an opener, exactly as advertised. 1.1 innings, 5 hitters, 25 pitches, and then Jose Urquidy for 3.2. Chicago's bullpen threw 7.2 of the 9 innings, which is the way that team is built and the thing the whole piece was about.

And the closing line of the pick was that I thought Detroit's bullpen would hold one more than Chicago's. Detroit's relievers threw 5.1 and gave up 3. Chicago's threw 7.2 and gave up 5. Per inning that's 5.06 against 5.87, so Detroit's pen was in fact the marginally better one on the night, same as the season numbers said it would be.

I won the argument I picked and it had nothing to do with the game. Both pens showed up after the score was 6-3, and the difference between them across 13 innings of mop-up was worth less than one inning of the starter.

The thing I said scared me is not what happened

Here's the whole section, and it's wrong in a specific way worth naming:

Detroit is 12-20 in 1 run games, 4th worst in baseball. That matters more than usual here, because a game where both teams empty the pen from the 5th inning on is exactly the kind of game that ends 4-3, and 4-3 is the score Detroit keeps losing.

It ended 9-5. There was never a moment after the 4th inning where a close-game record was going to decide anything.

That's the second night in a row I want to write about, because I've now leaned on the 1-run record twice and neither game was close. It's a real weakness and it's on the board, but naming it as the danger in a specific game is a different claim, and in this one it bought nothing. The danger was a starter with 5 innings on his arm.

The pattern the whole pick rested on broke

The season series had gone 3-3 and every one of the 6 games went to the home team. Chicago swept Detroit in Chicago in May, Detroit swept Chicago at Comerica in June, and 4 of the 6 were decided by 1 run.

That was the tidiest thing in the entry and it's the reason I liked Detroit: Chicago is 37-24 at home and 25-34 on the road, and this game was at Comerica.

Chicago won at Comerica. The series is 4-3 Chicago, the home team is 6-1 instead of 6-0, and the one number I built a call on stopped being true in the first game after I published it. A 6 game pattern is 6 games, and I knew that when I wrote it down, and I used it anyway because it was clean.

Detroit's offense was not the problem, which is new

10 hits and 5 runs against a staff that pitched 5 different arms. Given that Riley Greene, Matt Vierling, Kerry Carpenter and James Outman are all on the injured list and Friday's outfield had two rookies in it, 5 runs is more than I would have guessed.

Detroit's rotation ERA came into the night at 3.30, the lowest of all 30 teams, and that is the team's entire identity this season. Friday they scored 5 and lost by 4, because the one start they got from a pitcher who isn't part of that rotation yet cost them 6 runs in under 4 innings.

Saturday is Troy Melton, who is part of it.

entry.title: You were right about 2008. Here is what happens when you put it back in.

The 3 worst regular seasons in the sample all came out of a perfect preseason. Both 0-16 seasons in NFL history, and the 1-15 Chargers. That's not a small thing to have left out, and it's the version of this the sub has been telling each other for 18 years.

Add the near misses and it gets worse. St. Louis went 4-0 in the 2011 preseason and 2-14. Washington went 4-0 in 2013 and 3-13. Arizona 2003, Philadelphia 2012 and the Giants in 2019 all went 4-0 in August and 4-12 after it.

And then the other Lions team

2011. Also 4-0 in the preseason. 10-6, and the playoffs.

Same franchise, same perfect August, 3 seasons apart, and the two outcomes are the worst season anybody has ever had and the first Lions playoff berth in 12 years. If you want to know why the correlation is what it is, that's the whole argument inside one team.

Detroit's average preseason over those 25 years is .497 and their average regular season is .401, which is its own joke: this franchise has been almost exactly a .500 team in August and nowhere near it afterwards.

Detroit on its own correlates at +.285, which looks like something and isn't. That's 25 dots. The 2 seasons that would move it most are 2008 and 2011, and they point opposite directions.

The answer, on 798 team-seasons

Won every preseason game68.475-.025

Correlation between preseason win rate and regular season win rate: +.106. Variance explained: 1.1 percent.

On 320 team-seasons it was 1.0 percent. On 798 it's 1.1 percent. Adding 2008, and 2011, and 476 other team-seasons, moves the answer by a tenth of a percentage point. The thing the post said is still the thing the data says.

The line that does not survive

Here's what does change, and it's the sentence people quoted.

The first version said teams that went undefeated in August (.466) did worse than teams that went winless (.475). That inversion was fun and it's gone. On the full sample it's .475 for the undefeated group against .473 for the winless group, which is a 2 point gap across 138 teams and means nothing at all.

Look at it a different way and the undefeated group stops being the story entirely. Share of teams that won 9 or more per 17 games:
